title: String Practice
summary: Solve top placement string algorithms: in-place two-pointer reversals, palindrome validation, anagram detection, non-repeating character search, and frequency counting.
learningOutcomes: Implement two-pointer string algorithms with O(1) auxiliary space
Solve anagram and frequency problems using fixed integer arrays
Optimize string search and processing pipelines

activities.title: Core Mechanics: String Practice

breakdown.details: Converging left and right indices allow checking or reversing strings in O(N) time with O(1) space.
int[26] array maps ch - 'a' to count character occurrences with zero object allocation overhead.
Increment frequency for string A, decrement for string B; all slots must end at 0.

steps.description: Initialize two pointers at opposite ends of the string.
Compare characters at left and right; early exit if they don't match.
Anagram check early-exits if lengths differ.
Single-pass loop increments counts for s1 and decrements for s2.

questions.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of checking a palindrome using two pointers compared to creating a reversed StringBuilder?
options: Two-pointer is O(1) space; StringBuilder is O(N) space
Two-pointer is O(N) space; StringBuilder is O(1) space
questions.explanation: Two pointers only use two primitive integer variables (O(1) space), whereas StringBuilder allocates a new object copying the entire string (O(N) space).

questions.question: How do you map a lowercase English character `'ch'` to an array index between 0 and 25?
What is the time complexity of checking if two strings of length $N$ are anagrams using an `int[26]` frequency array?
questions.explanation: A single pass through both strings takes $O(N)$ time. Checking the 26 slots takes $O(26) = O(1)$ constant time. Overall complexity is $O(N)$.

questions.question: Which method from java.lang.Character checks if a character is alphanumeric (either a letter or a digit)?
questions.explanation: `Character.isLetterOrDigit(char ch)` returns true if ch is an alphabetic letter or numeric digit.

questions.question: What will `new StringBuilder("racecar").reverse().toString().equals("racecar")` evaluate to?
questions.explanation: "racecar" is a palindrome; its reverse is identical to itself, returning true.

questions.question: How can you find the first non-repeating character in a string in $O(N)$ time?
options: Use a frequency map/array on pass 1, then find the first character with count == 1 on pass 2
Use nested loops checking indexOf and lastIndexOf
questions.explanation: Two passes: pass 1 counts frequencies in an int[] array; pass 2 inspects characters in order and returns the first one whose count is 1.

questions.question: What is the result of `"listen".equals("silent")`?
options: false, because equals() checks exact character order
questions.explanation: .equals() checks identical character order. Even though they are anagrams, their sequences differ, so .equals() is false.

questions.question: What is the simplest way to remove duplicate adjacent spaces from a string?
questions.explanation: replaceAll("\\s+", " ") collapses all sequences of one or more whitespace characters into a single space.
s.toCharArray() creates an independent copy of the character array. Mutating `arr[0]` does not affect `s`, so output is "Java Kava".

questions.question: How do you count the number of vowels in a lowercase string in one pass?
options: Loop over characters and check if "aeiou".indexOf(ch) != -1
questions.explanation: Checking if "aeiou".indexOf(ch) != -1 (or using a switch) tests for vowels in $O(1)$ constant time per character.

questions.question: Why is toCharArray() useful for custom string algorithms?
options: It allows modifying the original String directly
It provides direct fast indexed array access `arr[i]` avoiding repeated bounds checks in charAt()
questions.explanation: toCharArray() returns a primitive char[] array that can be manipulated and swapped in place.

practice.title: Hands-On: Test Anagram Checker
practice.description: Check if "listen" and "silent" are anagrams using an int[26] array.

interviewQA.question: What is the optimal way to check if a string is a palindrome in Java?
interviewQA.answer: The two-pointer technique. By maintaining `left = 0` and `right = length - 1`, characters are compared moving inward. This requires $O(N)$ time and strictly $O(1)$ auxiliary space, avoiding the memory allocation overhead of creating a reversed copy with `StringBuilder`.

interviewQA.question: How do you check if two strings are anagrams in O(N) time and O(1) space?
interviewQA.answer: If lengths differ, return false immediately. Use an `int[26]` frequency array. In a single loop through the strings, increment `array[s1.charAt(i) - 'a']++` and decrement `array[s2.charAt(i) - 'a']--`. Finally, verify that all 26 elements are zero. Time complexity is $O(N)$ and space is $O(1)$ constant.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between str.toCharArray() and manual charAt() in performance?
interviewQA.answer: `str.toCharArray()` allocates a new `char[]` and copies characters into it, consuming $O(N)$ memory. However, accessing `arr[i]` avoids method call overhead and can be modified in-place for two-pointer swaps. `str.charAt(i)` allocates zero memory, but each call incurs a boundary check.

interviewQA.question: How do you find the first non-repeating character in a String with 1 million characters?
interviewQA.answer: Use an `int[256]` array (or a `LinkedHashMap<Character, Integer>` for full Unicode). In pass 1, iterate through the string and count frequencies. In pass 2, iterate through the string again in original order and return the first character whose frequency count is 1. This guarantees $O(N)$ linear time.

interviewQA.question: How would you reverse the words in a sentence without using split()?
interviewQA.answer: Convert the string to a `char[]`. First, reverse the entire character array. Second, iterate through the array and reverse each individual word between space boundaries. Finally, construct a new String. This operates in $O(N)$ time with minimal allocation.

interviewQA.question: Can two different strings have the same hashCode() in Java?
interviewQA.answer: Yes. This is called a **hash collision**. For example, in Java, `"FB".hashCode()` and `"Ea".hashCode()` both evaluate to `2236`. Because the output space of `int` is $2^{32}$ while the number of possible strings is infinite, collisions are inevitable (Pigeonhole Principle).

interviewQA.question: How does Java calculate the hashCode() of a String?
interviewQA.answer: Java uses the polynomial rolling formula: `s[0]*31^(n-1) + s[1]*31^(n-2) + ... + s[n-1]`. The prime number 31 was chosen because multiplication by 31 can be optimized by compilers into a bitwise shift and subtraction: `31 * x == (x << 5) - x`.

interviewQA.question: What is the Boyer-Moore string search algorithm?
interviewQA.answer: Boyer-Moore is a sublinear pattern search algorithm that skips character alignments from right to left using bad-character and good-suffix shift heuristics. In practice, it searches long texts in $O(N / M)$ average time, outperforming naive $O(N \times M)$ search.
